subject: ventures/dining-room-table-mix-optimizer
professional: a restaurant general manager or front-of-house operations consultant who plans floor layouts and table mixes; first checks: does the mix match the party-size distribution from POS/reservation data, are parties seated at the smallest fitting table, which tables can really be combined (adjacency, not any two), are turn times by party size used, is seat utilisation / covers per seat-hour visible, and does the recommendation survive a change of assumptions

evidence.correctness: Wrote an independent naive event simulator (per-physical-table busy-until times, smallest-fit single table, then fewest-seat pair, FCFS-fit waiting line with patience) in /tmp/claude-0/tm.mjs and ran it on 300 services from drawServices(seed 4242): today's 14 4-tops 106.243 guests/service naive vs 106.243 tool; recommended [10,8,0,0] 120.603 vs 120.603, exact. Erlang-B by direct sum (not the author's recursion) E(A=8,c=10) = 0.1217 vs simulator blocking 0.1176 over 12,609 parties (/tmp/claude-0/tm2.mjs; small low bias from empty-room start). Demand 62 x 3.14 mean party = 194.68 guests matches; monthly revenue 13.5167 x $34 x 40 = $18,382.67 and contribution x 0.30 = $5,514.80 match; lognormal multiplier exp(0.3Z - 0.045) has mean 1, CV sqrt(e^0.09 - 1) = 0.307 as the README says. Exhaustive enumeration of all 944 feasible mixes under 460 sq ft and the caps: with combine=yes the tool's [10,8,0,0] is the global optimum on its own search set (119.35). But with combine=no (one input changed) the steepest-ascent search stops at [3,11,1,0] = 111.22 search / 112.28 report, while the enumerated best [7,7,2,0] gives 115.10 / 116.71, 4.4 guests a service (about $6,000 a month at the example's $34 x 40) better; even the combine=yes mix [10,8,0,0] scores 114.00 under no-combining, beating the tool's own no-combine answer. A headline 'seats the most guests' output is wrong in a reachable configuration, so 2.
evidence.completeness: Every README/page feature works end to end on the example (node /tmp/claude-0/tm.mjs, 181 ms): current vs recommended mix table, guests per service with paired SE (13.52 +/- 0.34), parties turned away (24.27 -> 18.22), mean wait (3.19 -> 2.27 min), floor and seats, demand guests, value of one more / one fewer table, monthly sales and contribution, CSV download (toCsv), 600-party cap with message, usage opt-out with DNT. No stubs or TODOs. served-copy.mjs: no placeholder or retired origin in llms.txt, sitemap, robots, canonicals. Not shown although computed: seatMinutes (seat utilisation) is accumulated in runService/evaluate but never displayed.
evidence.verification: cd ventures/dining-room-table-mix-optimizer && node --test '*.test.mjs': 26 pass, 0 fail, 1.3 s. Good: an Erlang-B closed-form test and a 2,400-run field-for-field equivalence test against the previous simulator. Five seeded mutants via quality_mutate.py: smallest-fit '>=' -> '>' caught; lognormal mean correction removed (stays 4.6% longer) SURVIVED; contribution marginPct/100 -> /10 SURVIVED; standard error sqrt(var/n) -> sqrt(var) SURVIVED; monthly revenue missing x servicesPerMonth SURVIVED. 1 of 5 caught: every money and uncertainty figure the user acts on is unpinned, and no test checks that search() reaches the optimum on a small enumerable case.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (415 lines), index.html script (138-188), tests. Clean single engine, binary-insert departure list, free counts per seat size with a documented skip rule proven by the pinned test, common random numbers, caching in search. Defects: silent fallbacks, combine is true for any text but 'no' ('nope' -> yes, calc.mjs:240); patience 'abc' -> 0 (everyone unseated leaves) and spend blank -> $0 revenue with no warning (calc.mjs:235-239); margin above 100 silently clamped (238); seatMinutes computed and dropped. Acceptable.
evidence.claims: Checked 7 claims. Backed: 'Nothing uploaded' (page.test greps for fetch/XHR/sendBeacon; none), disclaimer and no-warranty footer plus 'Not decided' section, 'Takes about a second' (0.18 s measured), 'hundreds of simulated services' (300 report + 60 search), 'paired gain with standard error' (calc.mjs:363-366), Erlang-B check (calc.test.mjs:15), lognormal CV 0.3 (recomputed 0.307). Not backed: 'get the number of 2-tops, 4-tops and 6-tops that seats the most guests' (index.html:7,58, README:3) is a local-search result and is 4.4 guests/service short of the optimum with combining off; nothing on the page says the mix is a local optimum. Example footprints (4-top 32 sq ft = 8 sq ft/seat) are labelled placeholders.
evidence.fitness: Walked the GM's job: enter floor area, table types with footprints and caps, party-size shares and turn times from POS, walk-in patience; get a recommended mix, the gain with uncertainty, turned-away parties and the marginal value of each table type. That finishes and is useful as a directional answer, better than the usual 'match the party-mix ratio' rule of thumb. Gaps a GM hits: combining assumes any two free tables anywhere can be pushed together (no adjacency or fixed pairs, no three-table combos), which drives the 2-top-heavy answer (the recommended mix loses 7.2 guests/service when combining is off); no seat-utilisation or covers-per-seat-hour (RevPASH) output although seatMinutes is computed; no reservations/holding tables; one busy service only.
evidence.domain: Party-size mix, turn time by party size, smallest-fitting-table seating, walk-away patience, common random numbers and paired standard errors are what a FOH operations analyst would build, and exceed the usual spreadsheet ratio method; the closest standard reference is Kimes and Thompson (2004, Decision Sciences, 'Restaurant revenue management at Chevys: determining the best table mix'), which also simulates walk-in demand to choose a mix. Departures: Thompson's work on dedicated vs combinable tables treats combining as limited to tables that can physically be joined, here any two free tables combine; objective is guests, not RevPASH (equivalent only with constant spend per guest, which the page states); example density of 8-10 sq ft per seat is below the common 12-15 sq ft/seat for full-service dining (labelled placeholder).

defects.what: Steepest-ascent search stops at a local optimum: on the example with combining off it recommends [3,11,1,0] (112.28 guests/service on the report set) while exhaustive enumeration of the 944 feasible mixes gives [7,7,2,0] (116.71), 4.4 guests a service or about $6,000 a month at the example's prices; the page promises the mix that seats the most guests. The space is small enough to enumerate (or add restarts) for typical inputs
Page and README say the tool returns the mix 'that seats the most guests' with no statement that it is a heuristic search result

Monthly sales, contribution and the standard error are untested: dropping x servicesPerMonth, /100 -> /10 on margin, and sqrt(var/n) -> sqrt(var) all leave 26 tests green; no test checks search optimality on an enumerable case

Combining lets any two free tables anywhere be pushed together (no adjacency or fixed combinable pairs), which a floor plan rarely allows; the 2-top-heavy recommendation loses 7.2 guests/service when combining is off
Silent fallbacks: any combine text but 'no' means yes, unparseable patience becomes 0 (no waiting), blank spend becomes $0 revenue, margin over 100 clamped, none warned
Seat-minutes (seat utilisation, the RevPASH denominator a GM reads first) are computed per service but never shown
Example footprints give 8-10 sq ft per seat, below the common 12-15 sq ft/seat for full-service dining (labelled placeholder, but it is the published example)

verdict: A well-built queueing simulator: an independent per-table simulator reproduces its guests per service exactly (106.243 and 120.603), its loss rate matches Erlang-B (0.1176 vs 0.1217), the money arithmetic and demand figures recompute, and with combining on its recommendation [10,8,0,0] is the global optimum of all 944 feasible mixes. But the search is steepest ascent and can stop short: turn combining off and it recommends [3,11,1,0], 4.4 guests a service (about $6,000 a month in the example) worse than the enumerated best [7,7,2,0], while the page promises the mix that seats the most guests. Tests pin the simulator well but not the outputs a GM acts on: 4 of 5 seeded bugs in revenue, contribution, SE and dwell survive. Combining any two tables is optimistic for a real floor. Correctness and claims 2, verification 1: does not meet the bar; finished (completeness 3).
